newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Tung, Patten welcome Jiang's handover visit.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung, Patten welcome Jiang's handover visit.

text.p: In a rare show of agreement, Hong Kong's present and future leaders each welcomed on Wednesday Chinese President Jiang Zemin's plan to attend the British colony's June 30 handover to China.
Departing British governor Chris Patten and his designated successor under Beijing's rule, Tung Chee-hwa, separately hailed the announcement though they clash on many aspects of the power transfer.

But Patten expressed regret over China's decision to swear in the new Hong Kong executive, legislative and judicial officials right after the handover, effectively scrapping democratic reforms, a move that has aroused Western concern.

Jiang's visit demonstrated "how much importance the Central (Chinese) Government attaches to Hong Kong's reunification with the motherland and I feel very honoured to have them taking part in these historic ceremonies," Tung said in a statement.
Jiang, accompanied by Premier Li Peng, will lead the Chinese delegation at a Sino-British ceremony marking Hong Kong's return after 156 years of colonial rule.

He will also attend a ceremony marking the swearing-in of a new Hong Kong government, including a provisional legislature hand-picked by Beijing, a move that worries the West and has prompted a U.S. boycott.
"I'm delighted they're intending to come to Hong Kong for the handover," Patten told reporters during a tour of the city's new Chek Lap Kok airport site.
Patten, among others, views the provisional legislature as a poor substitute for Hong Kong's existing, democratically elected legislature.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright will attend the handover but has vowed to boycott that portion of the ceremony devoted to the swearing in of the provisional legislature, a decision which other VIP guests may imitate.
Patten denied that he had urged any foreign dignitaries to follow Albright's lead.
"What I think the rest of the world recognises is that we have in Hong Kong a legislature fairly elected...I think that they draw their own conclusions about China's policy on these matters."

"I think it would have been better -- and wiser counsel may still prevail -- if as would customarily happen the provisional legislature was being sworn in apart from the executive and judiciary," he said, citing the practice of the American and British governments.
"I think it would be sensible if those arrangements were looked at again but of course it's not a matter for me."
Britain, which will be represented at the handover ceremony by a delegation led by Britain's heir to the throne Prince Charles, welcomed Jiang's participation.

"The Chinese side of course has already informed us of the participation of the President of the People's Republic of China," Bill Dickson, British Foreign Office spokesman in Hong Kong, told Reuters.
"I think this underlines the importance that they attach to a successful handover and of course we very much welcome that."
But he would not comment on the participation of other Chinese officials.

Emily Lau, a pro-democracy Hong Kong legislator and an outspoken critic of Beijing, refrained from attacking the participation of Li Peng, widely seen accountable for the crushing of Beijing's 1989 Tiananamen Square democracy movement.
"I am not very surprised. I think all along we expected people like that to come," Lau told Reuters. "It's not for me to say happy or not really. They come whether we like it or not."
